source.title: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
source.authors: Chris Olah; Nick Cammarata; Ludwig Schubert; Gabriel Goh; Michael Petrov; Shan Carter

record.file_problem: none; full text of the essay present, figures not visible
record.tranche_reason: Original source for the claim. It describes the 4e:55 neuron and a car/dog superposition circuit by feature visualization and weight inspection. No systematic measurement.
record.gate_note: The essay is an original source for V1 and V3 and gets no labels. The 4e:55 example is re-presented from Feature Visualization (cited earlier work). It is recorded as a row because the essay states what the visualization shows. The seven curve-detector arguments concern a clean feature, not polysemanticity, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The config names this essay as the original source for V1. Its own qualitative results bear on V1 and V3. The first is the 4e:55 neuron in InceptionV1, which responds to cat faces, car fronts and cat legs; it is shown again from Feature Visualization (2017) and examined by feature visualization. The second is a new circuit in which a pure car feature in mixed4c is spread over next-layer neurons that mainly detect dogs, which the authors call superposition. There are no counts, shares or controls, and the figures are not in the text. The record's relation "discusses" and tranche T2 are corrected. The essay presents its own results, and as the original it uses the original method by definition.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is mostly right but needs correcting. The essay's main conclusions are its three speculative claims: features, circuits and universality. Polysemanticity is a caveat. On it, the authors say networks often contain polysemantic neurons that respond to unrelated inputs. One example is 4e:55, which they say is not detecting a shared cat/car feature. They call such neurons a major challenge to circuits analysis. The neurons seem to result from superposition: a circuit spreads a feature over many neurons, presumably to pack more features into limited neurons, as when a car feature is mixed into dog neurons. The authors hope to resolve polysemantic neurons themselves (not superposition as such) by 'unfolding' networks or by training networks to avoid polysemanticity. Separately, they hold that the typical neuron, or direction, is understandable. This is based on their study so far; it is not stated as an expectation.
record.recipe_differences: Original qualitative essay; no replication of a measure.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors state that thousands of hours studying individual neurons led them to believe the typical neuron, or sometimes another direction, is understandable. Polysemantic neurons are presented as the exception. This is an unquantified assertion with no count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Most neurons in vision models such as InceptionV1 are understandable on close study, and polysemantic neurons are a minority. This belongs to neurons_already_clean.

record.problems: Anecdotal, one neuron and one circuit. No prevalence figures. Figures not visible in the text. The superposition explanation is speculative.

untested.parts: No verdict, because this essay is the configured original. It shows one neuron (4e:55), re-presented from Feature Visualization 2017. There is no count or share of polysemantic neurons and no other vision model.
Not studied. Only InceptionV1 and other vision models are discussed; there are no language models.

Not tested: whether the network represents more features than it has neurons (capacity pressure), whether car and dog features are sparse or rarely co-occur, and how many polysemantic neurons arise this way. The reason is stated as belief, backed by a geometric footnote on almost-orthogonal vectors.
Not studied. There is no varying of initialization, regularization or neuron count.
Not studied. The authors only hope that networks could be trained not to be polysemantic, or 'unfolded'.
Not tested. The essay gives the original feature-visualization reading of 4e:55 (no shared feature), which V6 disputes. It does no reanalysis with better tools.
Not studied. Activation ranges and scoring of explanations are not examined.

record.verdict_notes: 1. Scope: the config lists this essay as an original for V1 only, so V1 gets no verdict. The record's gate_note says it is also an original for V3. This essay is in fact where the 'superposition' account of polysemantic neurons was first put forward. If Iris widens its originals scope to V3, the V3 'supports' label should be dropped. 2. V6 decision: the essay explicitly rejects a shared feature for 4e:55, but only by feature visualization. V6 claims that better tools overturn exactly this reading. Counting it as 'challenges V6' would treat the disputed original as evidence against its own reanalysis, so V6 is left untested and R2 is set to cannot_determine. 3. The 4e:55 evidence comes from the same group's Feature Visualization (2017). The figures (feature visualizations, weights) are not in the extracted text. 4. The glossary separates polysemantic neurons from 'real' multifaceted units such as the pose-invariant dog head, which unions over left and right cases. This is a definition, not a result, but it is relevant context for V6. 5. Independence: Cammarata co-wrote this essay and later the main challenge. 6. The text contains no instructions to the reader model.

versions.untested_parts: Only one example neuron (4e:55) is given. No count or share of polysemantic neurons.
One qualitative circuit example (car detector spread over dog-related neurons). No quantitative test of capacity pressure.
Only the one neuron 4e:55 is examined, by feature visualization. No better-tool reanalysis.

rows.check: Based on feature visualization, the authors say 4e:55 is not detecting a shared cat/car feature; it looks for cat eyes and whiskers, furry legs and shiny car fronts. That is the original reading V6 says better tools overturn. Feature visualization alone cannot show V6's effect, and no reanalysis is done, so 'absent' is changed to cannot_determine. The row also confirms the 'unrelated inputs' part of V1, which R1 already covers. It partly re-presents Feature Visualization 2017.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: weight-level circuit inspection of the mixed4c car neuron and its downstream neurons
rows.measure: how the car feature is carried into later layers
rows.value: car feature is spread over neurons that mainly detect dogs; authors call this superposition
rows.note: Qualitative single example. The reason (saving neurons, cars and dogs rarely co-occur) is stated as belief, not tested.
rows.check: The link is correct. Weight inspection of one circuit shows the mixed4c car neuron's feature mixed into next-layer neurons that mainly detect dogs. That makes them polysemantic, and the authors call it deliberate. This is qualitative, a single circuit, and the figures are not in the text. The causal part of V3 is not tested: saving neurons, the condition that cars and dogs don't co-occur, and the footnote 7 geometric argument are all stated as belief. The row note already says so.

source_check.problem: The text points to figures of the car neuron and the dog detectors. 'Weight-level inspection' is the record's gloss of the circuits method. The cause (using fewer neurons) is stated as belief.
